name: Kenta Iwamoto Foot Sweep System
description: Study foot sweeps and leg trips with a focused Kenta Iwamoto course match, practical partner drills, clear decisions, and ways to review your progress.
summary: The Kenta Iwamoto Foot Sweep System connects standing grips and changes of balance to small inside and outside leg attacks, then develops related clinch combinations.
overview:
Standing practice becomes easier to review when a foot sweep is treated as a timing problem rather than a kick at an available ankle. Watch how the opponent steps, where the weight moves, and whether your upper-body connection supports the intended direction. Controlled partner movement is useful before full takedown rounds.

Samurai Foot Sweeps & Leg Trips by Kenta Iwamoto is the matched instructional. Iwamoto covers kouchi and kosoto mechanics, grip fighting, and over-under combinations including sasae and uchi mata. The drills, sequence, and assessment criteria below are an original BJJGraph study plan; use them to organize practice alongside the course and feedback from a coach.
key_principles: Observe the step and weight change before attempting the sweep.
Use upper-body connection to support the intended direction.
Keep your own stance available after an unsuccessful entry.
Distinguish an inside target from an outside target.
Agree on controlled falling and reset conditions before increasing speed.

key_components.purpose: Connect an attack to a visible timing cue.

key_components.description: Choose one tie and test whether you can influence the partner's step without pulling yourself out of balance.
key_components.purpose: Relate the hand connection to the lower-body opportunity.

key_components.description: Alternate the partner's stance and select one reviewed inside or outside leg attack, stopping if the target is no longer available.
key_components.purpose: Build a two-option decision from actual movement.

key_components.description: After an unsuccessful entry, return to balanced contact or a coach-approved second attack rather than forcing the first one.
key_components.purpose: Keep combinations connected to changing balance.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The sweep strikes a heavily planted foot.
common_obstacles.solution: Slow down and identify the weight-transfer cue before attempting the entry.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The upper-body pull breaks your own stance.
common_obstacles.solution: Rehearse the tie and stepping pattern without completing a takedown.

common_obstacles.obstacle: You keep chasing a leg after the target changes.
common_obstacles.solution: Reset to balanced contact or choose a reviewed second option.
Return to cooperative falling practice with a coach before adding resistance.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: BJJGraph practice suggestion: With a partner walking at a cooperative pace, call the target step before attempting a light sweep entry without completing the fall. Then connect it to upper-body connection. Compare the first lost control point after each round. Keep the first repetitions cooperative and agree on resistance, space, and reset conditions. Once the starting task is clear, add one defensive option at a time and compare the result with the intended control objective.

flashcards.question: What makes foot-sweep timing worth isolating?
flashcards.answer: A visible step and weight change give you a more useful cue than simply reaching for any nearby ankle.

flashcards.question: What should the upper-body connection contribute?
flashcards.answer: It should support the intended direction and influence the step without pulling you out of your own stance.

flashcards.question: How can early practice avoid forcing complete throws?
flashcards.answer: Call the target step and rehearse a light entry at cooperative speed, stopping before the fall when appropriate.

flashcards.question: When should you switch from an inside to an outside option?
flashcards.answer: Switch when the stance and available target support the reviewed alternative rather than chasing the original leg.

flashcards.question: What should happen after a failed sweep entry?
flashcards.answer: Recover balanced contact or use a coach-approved continuation that matches the opponent's changed position.

flashcards.question: What should be established before live foot-sweep rounds?
flashcards.answer: Partners should have suitable mats, controlled falling practice, and clear intensity and reset conditions.
